source: MIT Museum: floor maps and OCEANS booklet (its file server); objects photographed in the museum, from Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Remembering the Future
artworks.description: A colored aerial sculpture of knotted fibre that floats through the lobby and over the grand stair, made during Echelman’s residency at MIT’s Center for Art, Science & Technology. You can see it from the lobby and from the stairs to the Second Floor.
artworks.galleryName: Lobby (free to enter)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo of the grand stair, Oct 2025, via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: MIT Museum Store
artworks.description: Books, kits, puzzles and MIT gifts. Free to enter; it keeps longer hours than the galleries.
artworks.galleryName: MIT Museum Store
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.

artworks.title: Sensing Oceans
artworks.description: How people and sea creatures sense the ocean: early oceanographic instruments, current MIT research and art by the collective Marshmallow Laser Feast, including Seeing Echoes in the Mind of the Whale and Plankton Temple. Part of the museum’s OCEANS season.
artworks.galleryName: Henri A. Termeer Gallery: Sensing Oceans (until Feb 21, 2027)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: Marshmallow Laser Feast, Plankton Temple, 2025; photo courtesy of the artist, from the museum’s OCEANS booklet

artworks.title: Crochet Coral Reef
artworks.medium: Crocheted yarn and other fibres; folded paper
artworks.description: Hand-crocheted corals by the Institute For Figuring and thousands of makers around the world: the hyperbolic shapes of real reef creatures, a lesson in geometry and a warning about climate change. With folded-paper sculptures by MIT’s Erik and Martin Demaine that find the same curves in paper.
artworks.galleryName: Exchange Gallery: Crochet Coral Reef (until Feb 14, 2027)
artworks.placeNote: The museum calls it the Exchange Gallery; it is taken to be the gallery beside The Exchange on the Second Floor (approximate).
artworks.imageCredit: Crochet Coral Reef, Museum Frieder Burda; photo Richard Nielsen, from the museum’s OCEANS booklet

artworks.title: Starship Enterprise model
artworks.description: The restored 33-inch model of the starship Enterprise made for the 1964 Star Trek pilot, lent by the Roddenberry family for its first showing on the East Coast. Shown near the Crochet Coral Reef, with a board on its story.
artworks.galleryName: Exchange Gallery: Crochet Coral Reef (until Feb 14, 2027)
artworks.placeNote: The museum calls it the Exchange Gallery; it is taken to be the gallery beside The Exchange on the Second Floor (approximate).

artworks.title: Essential MIT
artworks.description: Essential MIT: the experimental culture of the MIT community, told through its research. Hands-on stations on space, climate, health and more; the museum’s opening exhibition in the new building.
artworks.galleryName: Brit J. and Alex d’Arbeloff Gallery: Essential MIT
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo Oct 2025, via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: LIGO 1.5 m prototype
artworks.description: Essential MIT: the experimental culture of the MIT community, told through its research. An early test version of the laser interferometer Rainer Weiss designed to catch gravitational waves. LIGO first heard two black holes merging in 2015, and Weiss shared the 2017 Nobel Prize.
artworks.galleryName: Brit J. and Alex d’Arbeloff Gallery: Essential MIT
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Squeezer (optical parametric oscillator)
artworks.description: Essential MIT: the experimental culture of the MIT community, told through its research. Used in the first tests of “squeezed light” at the LIGO observatory in Hanford: a quantum trick that lowers noise so the detectors can hear fainter gravitational waves.
artworks.galleryName: Brit J. and Alex d’Arbeloff Gallery: Essential MIT
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Plasma Science Experiment, flight spare for Voyager 1 and 2
artworks.description: Essential MIT: the experimental culture of the MIT community, told through its research. The spare of the instrument MIT built to measure the solar wind on the Voyager probes, which are still sending data from interstellar space.
artworks.galleryName: Brit J. and Alex d’Arbeloff Gallery: Essential MIT
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Scalable tactile glove
artworks.description: Essential MIT: the experimental culture of the MIT community, told through its research. A cheap glove covered in pressure sensors that taught a neural network to recognise objects by touch.
artworks.galleryName: Brit J. and Alex d’Arbeloff Gallery: Essential MIT
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Cooling-tower water capture prototype
artworks.description: Essential MIT: the experimental culture of the MIT community, told through its research. A lab-scale model of a system that catches the water lost as plumes from power-plant cooling towers.
artworks.galleryName: Brit J. and Alex d’Arbeloff Gallery: Essential MIT
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Jenga-playing robot
artworks.description: Essential MIT: the experimental culture of the MIT community, told through its research. A robot arm that learned to play Jenga by feel as well as by sight, pushing blocks gently and sensing when they resist.
artworks.galleryName: Brit J. and Alex d’Arbeloff Gallery: Essential MIT
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Made to Measure
artworks.description: Made to Measure: a case of measuring instruments from the collection, at the top of the grand stair. Instruments that measure heat, humidity, strain, electricity and distance, and the Smoot: the unit Oliver Smoot’s classmates used to measure the Harvard Bridge in 1958.
artworks.galleryName: Top of the grand stair: Made to Measure display case
artworks.placeNote: In the Made to Measure case at the top of the grand stair (the instruments in it are approximate).

artworks.title: Ammonia maser
artworks.description: Made to Measure: a case of measuring instruments from the collection, at the top of the grand stair. One of the first masers, the microwave ancestor of the laser, built by James Gordon (MIT class of 1949) with Charles Townes at Columbia.
artworks.galleryName: Top of the grand stair: Made to Measure display case
artworks.placeNote: In the Made to Measure case at the top of the grand stair (the instruments in it are approximate).
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Kelvin’s electric balance
artworks.description: Made to Measure: a case of measuring instruments from the collection, at the top of the grand stair. A precise balance that weighs the pull between two coils to measure an electric current.
artworks.galleryName: Top of the grand stair: Made to Measure display case
artworks.placeNote: In the Made to Measure case at the top of the grand stair (the instruments in it are approximate).
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Transit theodolite
artworks.description: Made to Measure: a case of measuring instruments from the collection, at the top of the grand stair. A surveyor’s instrument for measuring angles, of the kind MIT civil engineering students learned on.
artworks.galleryName: Top of the grand stair: Made to Measure display case
artworks.placeNote: In the Made to Measure case at the top of the grand stair (the instruments in it are approximate).
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Model G pH meter
artworks.description: Made to Measure: a case of measuring instruments from the collection, at the top of the grand stair. Arnold Beckman’s acidity meter, the first of its kind sold commercially, which began the business of electronic lab instruments.
artworks.galleryName: Top of the grand stair: Made to Measure display case
artworks.placeNote: In the Made to Measure case at the top of the grand stair (the instruments in it are approximate).
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Maker Hub
artworks.description: Drop-in activities every day, led by museum staff and free with admission: build, tinker and test ideas. The Learning Labs next door hold workshops for groups.
artworks.galleryName: Maker Hub: hands-on drop-in activities (free with admission)
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.

artworks.title: Split | Second
artworks.description: Part of the TIME season: instruments and artworks in four sections, Earth Time, Mechanical Time, Electric Time and Atomic Time, on how we have measured ever smaller slices of a second.
artworks.galleryName: Martin J. and Eleanor C. Gruber Gallery: changing exhibitions
artworks.placeNote: Which gallery the show is in is a guess: the Gruber Gallery holds changing exhibitions.

artworks.title: AI: Mind the Gap
artworks.description: AI: Mind the Gap: what machines can and cannot do, from Claude Shannon’s game-playing machines to today’s robots and neural networks. Train a robot, watch a neural network think in real time, and write a poem together with an AI.
artworks.galleryName: AI: Mind the Gap
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.

artworks.title: Kismet
artworks.artist: Cynthia Breazeal, MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
artworks.description: AI: Mind the Gap: what machines can and cannot do, from Claude Shannon’s game-playing machines to today’s robots and neural networks. A robot head with eyebrows, ears and lips that read people’s faces and voices and answered with its own expressions: one of the first “social robots”.
artworks.galleryName: AI: Mind the Gap
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Theseus
artworks.description: AI: Mind the Gap: what machines can and cannot do, from Claude Shannon’s game-playing machines to today’s robots and neural networks. A mechanical mouse that finds its way through a maze and remembers the route: one of the first machines that learned. Claude Shannon, the father of information theory, built it with his wife Betty.
artworks.galleryName: AI: Mind the Gap
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Nimwit
artworks.description: AI: Mind the Gap: what machines can and cannot do, from Claude Shannon’s game-playing machines to today’s robots and neural networks. A machine that plays the game of Nim, and nearly always wins.
artworks.galleryName: AI: Mind the Gap
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Endgame
artworks.description: AI: Mind the Gap: what machines can and cannot do, from Claude Shannon’s game-playing machines to today’s robots and neural networks. A small machine that plays the end of a chess game: Shannon also wrote the first paper on how a computer could play chess.
artworks.galleryName: AI: Mind the Gap
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: W. C. Fields juggling machine
artworks.description: AI: Mind the Gap: what machines can and cannot do, from Claude Shannon’s game-playing machines to today’s robots and neural networks. A little figure that bounce-juggles three balls on a drum, named after the comedian who started as a juggler. Shannon was a keen juggler himself.
artworks.galleryName: AI: Mind the Gap
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Red-Black
artworks.description: AI: Mind the Gap: what machines can and cannot do, from Claude Shannon’s game-playing machines to today’s robots and neural networks. Another of Shannon’s game-playing machines.
artworks.galleryName: AI: Mind the Gap
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: MIT Collects
artworks.description: MIT Collects: hundreds of objects from the museum’s collection of about 1.5 million, in lit glass cases along a 90-foot wall, arranged by topic. Its sections include Modeling Everything, A Sequence of Actions (early computing), Technology and the Dream (the Black experience at MIT) and Totally Useless Things.
artworks.galleryName: Edward O. Thorp Collections Gallery: MIT Collects
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo Oct 2025, via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Whirlwind computer (part)
artworks.description: MIT Collects: hundreds of objects from the museum’s collection of about 1.5 million, in lit glass cases along a 90-foot wall, arranged by topic. A section of Whirlwind, the first computer fast enough to work in real time; it led to magnetic-core memory and the SAGE air-defence network.
artworks.galleryName: Edward O. Thorp Collections Gallery: MIT Collects
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo Oct 2025, via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Integrator unit of the Differential Analyzer
artworks.description: MIT Collects: hundreds of objects from the museum’s collection of about 1.5 million, in lit glass cases along a 90-foot wall, arranged by topic. Part of Vannevar Bush’s room-sized mechanical computer, which solved equations with turning shafts and wheels.
artworks.galleryName: Edward O. Thorp Collections Gallery: MIT Collects
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Apollo Primary Guidance, Navigation and Control System (Block II prototype)
artworks.description: MIT Collects: hundreds of objects from the museum’s collection of about 1.5 million, in lit glass cases along a 90-foot wall, arranged by topic. MIT designed the computer and guidance that flew the Apollo spacecraft to the Moon. This prototype of the command module’s system includes the Apollo Guidance Computer.
artworks.galleryName: Edward O. Thorp Collections Gallery: MIT Collects
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Apollo Inertial Measurement Unit (test unit)
artworks.description: MIT Collects: hundreds of objects from the museum’s collection of about 1.5 million, in lit glass cases along a 90-foot wall, arranged by topic. The gyroscope ball that told Apollo which way it was pointing, built for vibration tests.
artworks.galleryName: Edward O. Thorp Collections Gallery: MIT Collects
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Minivac 601 computer kit
artworks.description: MIT Collects: hundreds of objects from the museum’s collection of about 1.5 million, in lit glass cases along a 90-foot wall, arranged by topic. A teaching kit of relays, switches and lights designed by Claude Shannon to show how computers work.
artworks.galleryName: Edward O. Thorp Collections Gallery: MIT Collects
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Solar cell prototype
artworks.description: MIT Collects: hundreds of objects from the museum’s collection of about 1.5 million, in lit glass cases along a 90-foot wall, arranged by topic. An early solar cell from MIT’s research on power from sunlight.
artworks.galleryName: Edward O. Thorp Collections Gallery: MIT Collects
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Nerd Kit
artworks.description: MIT Collects: hundreds of objects from the museum’s collection of about 1.5 million, in lit glass cases along a 90-foot wall, arranged by topic. A joke gift set from the 1990s: a tongue-in-cheek look at the “nerd” image of MIT students.
artworks.galleryName: Edward O. Thorp Collections Gallery: MIT Collects
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Freezing Time: Edgerton and the Beauty of the Machine Age
artworks.description: Doc Edgerton’s strobe and high-speed flash photographs from the 1930s, which froze a milk drop, a bullet and a hummingbird’s wings, with the stroboscopes he invented at MIT.
artworks.galleryName: Ronald A. and Carol S. Kurtz Photography Gallery
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.

artworks.title: Water Lines
artworks.description: Opens Dec 17, 2026. Where people meet water, by design: drawings from the museum’s collection of more than 8,000 MIT architecture thesis drawings, over 150 years, with work by recent graduates. Part of the OCEANS season.
artworks.galleryName: Ronald A. and Carol S. Kurtz Photography Gallery
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map and its descriptions put it.
artworks.imageCredit: Arthur V. Edwards, A Quarantine Hospital, MIT architecture thesis, 1889; MIT Museum
